claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has an as-cast lamellar FCC + B2 dual-phase microstructure.
Low-temperature annealing can precipitate ordered L12 intermetallic particles within the FCC phase.
The L12 precipitates produced by annealing are coherent and nanoscale.
Low-temperature annealing that produces coherent nanoscale L12 precipitates will simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
Fine L12 precipitates obstruct dislocation motion through Orowan bowing and bypass.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the L12 precipitates increases yield strength.
The nanoscale precipitates refine the microstructure.
The precipitates create effective phase boundaries.
A uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates produces a more homogeneous distribution of plastic strain.
More homogeneous plastic-strain distribution enhances ductility.
Annealing may improve yield strength by an amount on the order of tens of percent relative to the as-cast baseline.
The annealed alloy will maintain or improve uniform ductility relative to the as-cast baseline.
The proposed improvement applies to eutectic HEAs with lamellar structures amenable to L12 precipitation.
Nonoptimized annealing can coarsen the precipitates and negate the intended ductility enhancement.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis requires an increase in ductility, whereas the predicted outcome allows ductility merely to be maintained.
The predicted outcome permits unchanged ductility, but the falsification rule requires a statistically significant increase in both strength and ductility.

The boundary excludes nonoptimized treatments that cause coarsening, while the falsification rule treats coarsening-induced ductility loss as a refutation rather than as an out-of-bound processing condition.
